source.title: Learning Curves for Noisy Heterogeneous Feature-Subsampled Ridge Ensembles

record.tranche_reason: Tests sample-wise double descent in linear ridge regression and linear-classifier settings, using a different model class and analysis from the original deep-network size sweeps.
record.gate_note: Results on sample-wise test error and double-descent peaks are included. Numerical values visible only in plots are not recoverable from the supplied text; cited results from other studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study derives and numerically checks sample-wise double descent in feature-subsampled linear regression, measures it in classifiers on fixed ResNext features, and tests its dependence on noise and regularization. These results test V3 and parts of V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that feature subsampling shifts interpolation peaks, heterogeneous ensembling can reduce or eliminate under-regularized double descent, and the usefulness of ensembling depends on noise, correlations and task structure. Their practical demonstrations train linear classifiers on fixed pretrained features.
record.recipe_differences: Uses analytical learning curves for feature-subsampled linear ridge regression and tests linear classifiers on fixed deep-network features; it does not sweep deep-network size or training epochs as in the original claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Peak location changes with the feature subsampling fraction; peak height and presence depend on regularization and homogeneous versus heterogeneous feature allocation. Noise scales also affect the learning curves and optimal ensemble size.

fits_no_version.finding: At λ = 0.1, homogeneous and heterogeneous regression ensembles have similar learning curves.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of heterogeneous feature allocation diminishes at stronger ridge regularization.

record.peer_reviewed: 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023)
record.problems: The replica-trick derivation is described by the authors as non-rigorous. Many plotted values are not numerically reported in the text. The practical classification results use pre-trained ResNext features and linear classifiers, not deep-network training.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant results omitted; reported plot values without stated numerical values are retained as qualitative rows where the text describes their outcome.

untested.parts: The reported double-descent curves vary sample size, rather than increasing model capacity through interpolation.
No single effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs and samples. Predicting P = N in linear models does not establish this account.
Triple or multiple descent is not established. Optimal-regularization results concern the specified linear ensemble settings and locally optimal member regularization.
No effective-parameter reparameterization converting double descent into a U-shaped curve.

missing.what: Separate the noiseless, fully observed exception: ν = 1 and ζ = 0 in equation (21) yields error 1 − α for α < 1 and zero for α > 1, without a divergent peak.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. V3 does not require deep networks, so its linear-model setting is tested scope rather than an untested clause. Peak locations follow ordinary sampled-feature counts here; that alone does not test V5 or V7. Numerical peak heights and exact model-by-model curve shapes cannot be recovered from the supplied figure text.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of deep-network model size and test error.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The reported tests concern sample size in linear regression or linear classifiers, not increasing the number of training examples near the interpolation threshold in deep networks.
The study examines sample-wise curves, not risk as model capacity grows past the interpolation point across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
The paper studies label/readout noise and regularization in its settings; it does not test triple or multiple descent.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective parameter measure is tested.

rows.subject: single linear regressor (k = 1)
rows.operation_detail: Analytically evaluated the sample-wise generalization-error curve as sample complexity α varies.

conditions.value: fraction ν; equation gives cases α < ν and α > ν

rows.measure: Generalization error (MSE) as a function of sample complexity α.
rows.value: For α < ν and α > ν, equation (21) gives separate expressions; the text states that error diverges as (α − ν)⁻¹ when α = ν. The authors identify explicit label noise (ζ > 0) or implicit label noise induced by feature subsampling (ν < 1) as possible sources of double descent.
rows.note: Analytical sample-wise curve; the paper states the peak is at the sample/feature interpolation threshold.
rows.check: Restrict the divergence claim to ν < 1 or ζ > 0. Equation (21) has no divergent peak when ν = 1 and ζ = 0; the row currently includes that exception.

source_check.correct: The peak diverges at α=ν when ν<1 or ζ>0. For ν=1 and ζ=0, error is 1−α for α<1 and zero for α>1; V3 is absent in that subcondition.
source_check.problem: The observed state covers a noiseless, fully observed exception without a peak.

rows.subject: linear ridge ensemble (k = 10)
rows.operation_detail: Compared sample-wise theoretical learning curves for homogeneous and heterogeneous feature subsampling.
